events.note: Congress appropriated $3,500 for a light at Stonington Harbor (Bulletin 1929)
First tower and detached stone house finished; builder Benjamin Chase of Newport
Bulletin 1929 says lighted in 1824; the USLHS record gives 1823 for establishment (see notes_for_editor)
Inspector found 22 feet of the original property swept away by the sea
Light moved back from the point and rebuilt with the old stones; 35 ft octagonal tower; John Bishop of New London did the removal
Sixth-order Fresnel lens replaced the lamps and reflectors
Discontinued when the breakwater light (25 ft iron tower, 4th-order red lens, first shown 1 Nov 1889) took over
Federal government built a keeper's house next to the old light for the breakwater lightkeeper (NRHP); the Bulletin says the old dwellings housed breakwater keepers until 1908
Historic Stonington says the old house housed breakwater-light keepers until 1909 (conflicts with 1908)
Sea wall at Stonington Point repaired; federal appropriation of 1911 ($500), work completed November 1915
Sold by the government with part of the reservation; Stonington Historical Society acquired it for $3,650
Opened as a lighthouse museum (the museum calls it the nation's first)
Closed for renovations from 4 October 2026; reopening planned May 2027

corrections.why: The standing tower is an octagonal stone tower (NRHP 1975; LighthouseFriends; USLHS 'Tower Shape: Octagonal'). The record's conical_masonry type does not match these sources.
The standing tower dates from 1840; the 1823 tower was taken down and its stones reused.

corrections.proposed: Historic Stonington (formerly the Stonington Historical Society)
corrections.why: The museum now operates under its current name.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The first tower (1823) and the standing octagonal tower (1840) are both in the record; the record's 'built 1823' describes the first tower, now removed. The 1840 rebuild reused its stones (NRHP; Bulletin 1929).

Not a disagreement once the towers are separated. LighthouseFriends gives ten whale-oil lamps in thirteen-inch reflectors for the 1823 tower; the nomination and LighthouseFriends both give eight lamps in sixteen-inch reflectors for the 1840 light (the nomination's 'original lighting equipment' is the standing 1840 building's system).

notes_for_editor: Checked this round against the sources. Bulletin 1929 PDF p. 25 read from the page image (printed p. 296): 'In 1822 Congress appropriated $3,500', 'constructed in 1823 and lighted in 1824', Benjamin Chase 'of Newport' as builder, Potter appointed 1823 at $300 a year, removal by John Bishop 'of New London' completed September 1840. The sentence about the buildings being used for breakwater keepers 'until 1908' is on PDF p. 26, so footnote 2 now cites pp. 25-26. Index PDF p. 31 and Commissioner 1916 scan p. 160 (printed p. 51) rechecked. NRHP 76002000 read: keeper's house attached and built of granite blocks; 1840 light with 8 lamps and 16-inch reflectors ('original lighting equipment' designed and supplied by I.W.P. Lewis); 1856 sixth-order lens; 1908 breakwater keeper's house; first house 'further down the point'. LighthouseFriends read: 1822 funding; Chase contract; 1823 tower with ten whale-oil lamps in 13-inch reflectors; 1840 light with eight lamps in 16-inch reflectors; lens 'one year later' after 1854 (i.e. 1855); Pendleton 1872-1890 in its head-keeper list; 25-foot iron breakwater tower 1 Nov 1889; 1925 sale; 1914 British attack. Museum page read: 7 Water Street; 1840 roof; seven keepers and families; 1909 breakwater keepers; 1925 purchase for $3,650; 1927 'the nation's first'; closed from 4 October 2026, reopening May 2027. The museum page does not say the tower is closed, so the story no longer says so. CONFLICTS LEFT OPEN: first light 1823 (USLHS establishment year) vs 1824 (Bulletin lighted); lens 1855 (LighthouseFriends) vs 1856 (NRHP, USLHS); Pendleton's last year 1889 (USLHS, Bulletin) vs 1890 (LighthouseFriends); keepers' house use until 1908 (Bulletin, NRHP) vs 1909 (museum); the 1823 contract ($2,500 in the Bulletin, roughly $3,000 in LighthouseFriends) is not used. PEOPLE: the NRHP names 'I.W.P. Lewis' as supplier of the 1840 lighting equipment; the Bulletin index names Winslow Lewis for the old lighthouse's lamps. The story does not treat them as one person because no source connects them. NOT VERIFIED: the NRHP listing year (the record says 1976) is not confirmed; the form is dated July 1975 and the story uses 1975 for the form. ROSTER: the nine USLHS lines (seven principal keepers, two contractors) match the keepers list; the contractors Bishop and Chase are not keepers. LighthouseFriends also lists George W. Beckwith, Joseph J. Fuller and Louis S. Poutray as later head keepers of the breakwater light; they are not on this station's roster and are not in the story. No storms, wrecks or rescues tied to this light were found in the sources read, so there is no storms chapter.
